title: ‘Rooting’ the commons: sharing lessons from Odisha, India and the South West of England
content:
A guest post by Amlan Mishra

A version of this post was presented at the ‘Law for the commons’ workshop at the Centre for Environmental Law and Sustainability (CELS), University of Bristol on 26 June, 2026 where several friends from Bristol Commons participated.

In this post, I hope to illuminate synergies between commons I study in Odisha, India and the commons we hope to grow in the city of Bristol – through commons movements in the city that I have been associated with. But what can I – a first-generation immigrant who moved to Bristol three years back – say about commons struggles in Bristol and the South West of England? All I can offer are some stories – some vignettes of my participation in these commons struggles. I hope to translate my PhD research which focuses on dispossession of forest commons in Odisha, India and use it as a vantage point to offer reflections from it.

title: Shrinking Giants, Part 6: Beyond Fossil Finance
content:
This is the sixth article in an 8-part series based on an essay by Ronan Murphy. The global economy runs on a simple logic: states must grow or be outcompeted, and those that fall behind lose their security. In a system where power still flows, ultimately, from the barrel of a gun, Ronan explores what this means for anyone hoping to build something different.

Part 1 (with a list of articles in the series) can be found here.

If the preceding sections have diagnosed the problem, that growth is politically constructed, ecologically destructive, and militarily enforced, then the question becomes what material infrastructure could actually sustain a different kind of economy?

The collaborative finance (CoFi) space offers a way through. The field is growing, diverse, and often poorly understood. It spans mutual credit, community currencies, cooperative banking, commons-based resource management, and a range of mechanisms for organising exchange and investment outside the logic of interest-bearing debt and speculative capital.

title: Bananas as money: taking CoFi (Collaborative Finance) on the road
content:
“I will argue that to have an abundant, sustainable and just economic system we need interest-free money at every level of organisation – international, national and local – to complement the scarce money we have now.”

Deirdre Kent, Healthy Money, Healthy Planet, 2005

“We are the most in-debt, obese, addicted and medicated adult cohort in U.S. history.”

Brené Brown, Ted Talk The Power of Vulnerability, 2010


On October 4th, hot on the heels of the Stroud Festival of Commoning, Matthew Slater and I ran a workshop for the Bristol Commons, on building collective financial power.

I am very grateful to Matthew for offering to do this with me, after I posted in a chat about a potential CoFi study group. He does not live in the UK, so it was great to take advantage of him being there.

With this post, we are also introducing a new Collaborative Finance section on this Substack focusing on finance and monetary systems, especially the kind mentioned in our introductory post on CoFi. You can subscribe to this section separately.

title: Agroecology as fertile ground (...for growing the commons)
content:
Agroecological practices being applied in Ankazobe, Madagascar. The land is managed with respect for its ecology – here, plants are grown in small holes to help them retain moisture and nutrients, which is needed in the dry, nutrient-poor ecology. Image from Cactus0625 on Wikimedia. This file is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 International license.

Depending on how often you stick your nose into the food and farming news cycle, you might have seen a bunch of terminology being flung about every which way. “Regenerative” is the current favourite plaything of a lot of talk from all kinds of political backgrounds (just a quick search reveals both traditional environmentalist groups like the Irish Green Party and right-wing MAHA mogul RFK Jr. say we should do regenerative agriculture). Add that to a long list of terms like sustainable, organic, cruelty-free…

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support our work.

…I can’t blame anyone for feeling like these things are just hollow buzzwords being slapped on packets of biscuits and cartons of eggs. It’s an understandable impulse. They often are.

title: Shrinking Giants, Part 5: From Leviathan to Gaia
content:
This is the fifth article in an 8-part series based on an essay by Ronan Murphy. The global economy runs on a simple logic: states must grow or be outcompeted, and those that fall behind lose their security. In a system where power still flows, ultimately, from the barrel of a gun, Ronan explores what this means for anyone hoping to build something different.

Part 1 (with a list of articles in the series) can be found here.

If there is one takeaway from the analysis so far, it is that the Westphalian nation-state system, built on sovereign competition, militarised borders, and GDP-maximisation, is poorly suited to navigate safe passage to a sustainable future.

The climate crisis, resource constraints, and the need for equitable development all overflow national boundaries, and our primary political units jealously guard their short-term self-interests.

title: The Emergency: why communities must govern environmental resources
content:
There are many global emergencies. But Julian Jones of Water21 believes they all share a single neglected cause— and that the beginnings of solutions can be found close to home.

Climate, public health, flooding, drought, social inequality, displacement and economic instability. Presented separately, they leave us individually helpless. Yet a common failure runs through nearly all of them—and the beginnings of a solution is within our collective grasp. That failure is a lack of care. Not simply caring about something as sympathy or sentiment. I mean practical, active care: accepting responsibility for the people, places and resources that sustain us. I first began to understand this as a child in Stroud, through the metaphor—and practical reality—of our declining local rivers.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support our work.

title: Why I choose to build commons, rather than being an ‘activist’
content:
This text started out as a thread on X, after which its author Dil Green padded it out to serve as a response to Ann Pettifor’s Substack post ‘It is Time to Storm the Gates of Private Power’. We believe that it can stand as an article in its own right, which is why we are posting it in lightly edited form below.

For clarity, despite my position that spending time trying to get nation-states (and indeed any institutions of equivalent scale) to address the omnicrisis is a (bad) waste of time, I do strongly believe that they should be addressing it, and that this would be the best way.

I just know they cannot – not in any useful, effective or timely way. And thus working as an activist will be a waste of your effort at the most crucial point in all of human history.

Nation-states will not be effective in addressing the omnicrisis which faces the whole of humanity and the whole of the biosphere.

To be specific around 'cannot' and 'could': nation-states could do many things – they still have significant control around money and policy, and could bring democratic legitimacy to tough choices.

title: The marriage of developers and local communities
content:
This is a guest post by Matthew Slater, sharing valuable lessons from his personal experience as a developer working with, and for, communities. It was originally published on the author’s personal blog on 17th August 2026, and has been lightly edited here.

In my travels I’ve met many activist software developers like myself, overflowing with energy and idealism for communities in general, but no community in particular. Many of them were creating a new kind of platform that addressed the concerns of the moment – privacy, security, sovereignty, serverless architecture etc. I don’t mean they were collaborating; I mean each was building their own platform. Once the platform was ready they embarked on a quest for users, or, which is harder, whole communities of users ready and able to migrate to the latest platform. After a few years they run out of physical or spiritual resources, and move on. It seemed to me a predictable waste of developer years, but more tragically, a lost opportunity for the communities they wanted to help.

title: Shrinking Giants, Part 4. Guns or butter: post-growth security in a world of great powers
content:
This is the fourth article in an 8-part series based on an essay by Ronan Murphy. The global economy runs on a simple logic. States must grow or be outcompeted, and those that fall behind lose their security. In a system where power still flows, ultimately, from the barrel of a gun, Ronan explores what this means for anyone hoping to build something different.

Part 1 (with a list of articles in the series) can be found here.

The old dilemma of “guns or butter” takes on new complexity in a post-growth context. In a world transitioning away from endless growth, the hope would be to drastically scale back militarism and invest in human and ecological well-being. After all, armies are themselves huge drivers of ecological ruin. The US military, for example, is one of history’s largest carbon polluters, emitting more greenhouse gases than many entire countries.

A key tenet of a post-growth vision is that true security comes not from arms, but from meeting people’s basic needs and protecting planetary life-support systems.

title: A Commoners’ Manifesto 2. How corporations capture the state, part 3: pestering and manipulation
content:
‘Real lobbying reform must end the practice of corporate lobbyists writing our laws.’ - Marty Meehan

‘Real lobbying reform must end the practice of corporate lobbyists writing our laws.’ - Marty Meehan

This is one of a series of articles that I hope to compile into a book – working title, The Commoners’ Manifesto: Neither Capitalism nor Communism. Here’s an introduction to the series. Comments welcome, including disagreement and debate.

I’ve argued that anti-capitalists should reject state communism as the route to a post-capitalist world, and that community-based, commons solutions are more likely to succeed. In fact I’m arguing that corporations have captured and now control the states that created them, so that a post-capitalist world can’t be built via a ‘democratic’ state either.

content:
By Amrit Sachar and Louise Romain, Festival Organisers

When we last wrote about the Festival of Commoning in July, the programme was still taking shape. It has now been published, and I am excited to give you a glimpse of what our programme team has created, with 17 contributors and 8 venues.

In the two days of programme, this year’s theme ‘Common Ground: Healing Divides’ will take you through innovative, grassroots projects from around the world, exploring neighbourhood organising, cooperative economies, land, food, energy, housing, democracy and governance.

title: Shrinking Giants, Part 3: Security gaps and lessons from Rojava
content:
This is the third article in an 8-part series based on an essay by Ronan Murphy. The global economy runs on a simple logic. States must grow or be outcompeted, and those that fall behind lose their security. In a system where power still flows, ultimately, from the barrel of a gun, Ronan explores what this means for anyone hoping to build something different.

Part 1 (with a list of articles in the series) can be found here.

Even if internal inequalities are managed, a post-growth community must survive in a hostile environment in the short and medium terms in order to scale. Today’s world is dominated by nation states vying over sovereignty and great powers jockeying for resources and influence. The question then becomes, how does a sustainable experiment hold its own amid the realpolitik.

title: Come to the third Festival of Commoning, in Stroud, Oct 2-3, 2026
content: In an age defined by division, inequality, and a deep-seated sense of isolation, the concept of “commoning” feels less like an archaic tradition and more like a radical, necessary blueprint for the future. It’s a powerful idea that reclaims the principle that some things – land, resources, community – should be ours to share, protect, and manage together. This October, the town of Stroud in the UK will become a vibrant hub for this idea, hosting the Festival of Commoning 2026 under the fitting theme, “Common Ground: Healing Divides.”

title: The farmland you didn't know you had
content: There is a very persistent problem in many of our lives, and this same problem is an issue that needs grappling with when trying to create new commons. This problem is access to land. Most people don’t own land, but instead rent it, which comes with restrictions on usage and a sense of impermanence. At the same time, both owners and renters can completely lack access to land that is usable for subsistence.
